claim: Chondrosarcomas are primary cancers of cartilaginous tissue capable of alteration to highly aggressive, metastatic, and treatment-refractory states.
source: Chondrosarcomas are primary cancers of cartilaginous tissue and capable of alteration to highly aggressive, metastatic, and treatment-refractory states, leading to a poor prognosis with a five-year survival rate at 11 months for dedifferentiated subtype.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a characterization of chondrosarcomas based on established medical knowledge.

claim: The five-year survival rate for dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma is 11 months.
source: Chondrosarcomas are primary cancers of cartilaginous tissue and capable of alteration to highly aggressive, metastatic, and treatment-refractory states, leading to a poor prognosis with a five-year survival rate at 11 months for dedifferentiated subtype.
evidence: This specific survival statistic is provided in the abstract as a factual claim about patient outcomes.

claim: Surgical resection of chondrosarcoma is the only effective treatment currently available.
source: At present, the surgical resection of chondrosarcoma is the only effective treatment, and no other treatment options including targeted therapies, conventional chemotherapies, or immunotherapies are available for these patients.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and reflects current clinical practice limitations.

claim: SULF1 is the top EZH2-targeted gene regulating chondrosarcoma progression.
source: A non-biased chromatin immunoprecipitation sequence, cDNA microarray analysis, and validation of chondrosarcoma cell lines identified sulfatase 1 (SULF1) as the top EZH2-targeted gene to regulate chondrosarcoma progression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ChIP-seq, microarray analysis, and validation experiments described in the abstract.

claim: Overexpressed EZH2 results in downregulation of SULF1 in chondrosarcoma cell lines.
source: Overexpressed EZH2 resulted in downregulation of SULF1 in chondrosarcoma cell lines, which in turn activated cMET pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing the relationship between EZH2 and SULF1 expression levels.

claim: Downregulation of SULF1 activates the cMET pathway in chondrosarcoma.
source: Overexpressed EZH2 resulted in downregulation of SULF1 in chondrosarcoma cell lines, which in turn activated cMET pathway.
evidence: This mechanistic relationship is demonstrated through experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Pharmaceutical inhibition of cMET significantly retards chondrosarcoma growth and extends mice survival.
source: Pharmaceutical inhibition of cMET or genetically silenced cMET pathway significantly retards the chondrosarcoma growth and extends mice survival.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experimental data using cMET inhibitors in mouse models.

claim: Genetic silencing of cMET pathway significantly retards chondrosarcoma growth and extends mice survival.
source: Pharmaceutical inhibition of cMET or genetically silenced cMET pathway significantly retards the chondrosarcoma growth and extends mice survival.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using genetic approaches to silence cMET in mouse models.

claim: The EZH2/SULF1/cMET axis is validated in patient samples with chondrosarcoma.
source: The regulation of EZH2/SULF1/cMET axis were further validated in patient samples with chondrosarcoma.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data from patient tissue samples.

claim: Chondrosarcoma is the most common primary skeletal malignancy affecting bone.
source: Chondrosarcoma, a malignant cartilaginous tumor, is the most common primary skeletal malignancy affecting bone (Editorial and Consensus Conference Working Group, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Chondrosarcomas are classified into primary central and secondary peripheral types based on their location in the bone.
source: They are further classified into primary central and secondary peripheral chondrosarcomas based on their location in the bone (Gelderblom et al., 2008).
evidence: This classification system is cited from published literature.

claim: The most common sites for chondrosarcoma are bones of the pelvis, followed by the diaphysis or metaphysis of the proximal femur and humerus, distal femur, and ribs.
source: The most common sites are bones of the pelvis, followed by the diaphysis or metaphysis of the proximal femur and humerus, distal femur, and ribs.
evidence: This anatomical distribution is stated as established medical knowledge.

claim: Histological grade is the best predictor of clinical behavior in chondrosarcomas.
source: They are the best predictor of clinical behavior at present (Evans et al., 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Metastasis is rare in Grade I chondrosarcomas.
source: Metastasis is rare in Grade I chondrosarcomas, while metastases occur in 10% of Grade II and 71% of Grade III chondrosarcomas (Björnsson et al., 1998).
evidence: This clinical observation is cited from published literature.

claim: Metastases occur in 10% of Grade II chondrosarcomas.
source: Metastasis is rare in Grade I chondrosarcomas, while metastases occur in 10% of Grade II and 71% of Grade III chondrosarcomas (Björnsson et al., 1998).
evidence: This specific metastasis rate is cited from published literature.

claim: Metastases occur in 71% of Grade III chondrosarcomas.
source: Metastasis is rare in Grade I chondrosarcomas, while metastases occur in 10% of Grade II and 71% of Grade III chondrosarcomas (Björnsson et al., 1998).
evidence: This specific metastasis rate is cited from published literature.

claim: Conventional chondrosarcomas are extremely resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy.
source: Conventional chondrosarcomas are extremely resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, resulting in limited treatment options (Choy et al., 2012; Gelderblom et al., 2008).
evidence: This clinical characteristic is cited from published literature.

claim: A therapeutic surgical approach remains the only practical treatment for chondrosarcoma depending on the grade.
source: Depending on the grade of the chondrosarcoma, a therapeutic surgical approach remains the only practical treatment (Lee et al., 1999).
evidence: This treatment approach is cited from published literature.

claim: 70% of chondrosarcoma patients are inoperable.
source: After surgery, patients with poor-quality life and for those inoperable patients (70%), radiation therapy alone is an option with uncertainty outcome (Fromm et al., 2018).
evidence: This statistic is cited from published literature.

claim: The relatively poor vascularity of chondrosarcomas results in more difficult drug delivery than to other vascularized cancers.
source: Additionally, the relatively poor vascularity results in more difficult delivering drugs than to other vascularized cancers (Bovée et al., 2010; Gelderblom et al., 2008; Lee et al., 1999).
evidence: This biological characteristic is cited from published literature.

claim: Lack of interest from pharmaceutical industry obstructs drug development and clinical trials for chondrosarcoma due to rarity and various subtypes.
source: Due to rarity and various subtypes of chondrosarcoma, lack of interest from pharmaceutical industry obstructs the drug development and conduct of clinical trials for these patients (Miwa et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim about pharmaceutical industry challenges is cited from published literature.

claim: There are no effective treatments for patients with inoperable or metastatic chondrosarcoma (70% of patients).
source: Until now, there are no effective treatments for patients with inoperable or metastatic disease (70%), and therefore, it is an un-met medical need to develop new treatment modalities.
evidence: This represents the current state of clinical practice and unmet medical need.

claim: IGF inhibitors increase the rate of apoptosis in chondrosarcomas.
source: IGF inhibitors have been used to treat chondrosarcomas by increasing the rate of apoptosis (Ho et al., 2009; Olmos et al., 2010).
evidence: This therapeutic mechanism is cited from published literature.

claim: Dasatinib reduces cell viability in chondrosarcoma cell lines by targeting SRC.
source: Small molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor dasatinib is known to reduce cell viability in chondrosarcoma cell lines by targeting SRC (Schrage et al., 2009).
evidence: This drug mechanism is cited from published literature.

claim: EZH2 is the major component of the polycomb repressor complex 2 (PRC2).
source: Enhancer of Zeste 2 (EZH2) is the major component of the polycomb repressor complex 2 (PRC2; Kuzmichev et al., 2002).
evidence: This molecular function is cited from published literature.

claim: PRC2 represses gene expression through EZH2-catalyzed trimethylation of histone 3 lysine 27 (H3K27).
source: PRC2 has been reported to repress gene expression through the histone methyltransferase EZH2-catalyzed trimethylation of histone 3 lysine 27 (H3K27) to establish repressive epigenetic marker (Cao et al., 2002; Cao and Zhang, 2004; Kuzmichev et al., 2002).
evidence: This molecular mechanism is cited from published literature.

claim: EZH2 is required to maintain DNA methylation and suppress specific genes through direct interaction with DNA methyltransferases (DNMT1, DNMT3A, and DNMT3B).
source: EZH2 is required to maintain DNA methylation and suppress specific genes such as tumor suppressor genes by direct interaction of EZH2 and DNA methyltransferases (DNMT1, DNMT3A, and DNMT3B; Sauvageau and Sauvageau, 2010).
evidence: This molecular mechanism is cited from published literature.

claim: Overexpression of EZH2 has been observed in lymphomas, sarcomas, and cancers of the breast, colon, liver, lung, and prostate.
source: Overexpression of EZH2 has been observed in lymphomas, sarcomas, and cancers of the breast, colon, liver, lung, and prostate (Chang and Hung, 2012; Han et al., 2020; Li et al., 2009; Sauvageau and Sauvageau, 2010; Yamaguchi and Hung, 2014).
evidence: This pattern of EZH2 overexpression across cancer types is cited from published literature.

claim: E2F transcription factors can bind to the promoters of EZH2 and EED, which is necessary for E2F-modulated cell proliferation.
source: It has been reported that EZH2 mediates different types of human cancer through transcriptional, post-transcriptional, and post-translational stages, demonstrating that transcriptional factors, such as E2F, are able to bind to the promoters of EZH2 and (Embryonic ectoderm development)EED, which is necessary for E2F modulated-cell proliferation (Bracken et al., 2003; Wei et al., 2011).
evidence: This transcriptional regulation mechanism is cited from published literature.

claim: EWS-FLI1 can transcriptionally activate EZH2 expression in Ewing's sarcoma.
source: EWS-FLI1, a fusion oncoprotein in Ewing's sarcoma, can transcriptionally activate EZH2 expression, and upregulated EZH2 expression plays a vital role in tumor growth and endothelial/neuroectodermal differentiation (Richter et al., 2009).
evidence: This regulatory mechanism in Ewing's sarcoma is cited from published literature.

claim: EZH2 directly targets KLF2, a tumor suppressor, and interrupts its functions in cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in osteosarcoma.
source: More recently, Taniguchi et al., 2012 demonstrated that EZH2 directly targets the Kruppel-like factor 2 (KLF2), which is a tumor suppressor, and interrupts its functions in cell cycle arrest and apoptosis, leading to tumorigenesis in the osteosarcoma mouse model (Taniguchi et al., 2012).
evidence: This molecular mechanism in osteosarcoma is cited from published literature.

claim: Dysregulation of differentiation programs of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) may lead to osteosarcomas and chondrosarcomas.
source: Notably, the dysregulation of differentiation programs of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) may lead to osteosarcomas and chondrosarcomas (Mohseny and Hogendoorn, 2011).
evidence: This developmental mechanism is cited from published literature.

claim: Human sulfatase 1 (SULF1) desulfates cellular heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs).
source: Human sulfatase 1 (SULF1) was characterized and revealed to desulfate cellular heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs).
evidence: This enzymatic function is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Sulfated HSPGs play a vital role in regulating heparin binding growth factor signaling including FGF2, VEGF, HGF, PDGF, and HB-EGF.
source: Sulfated HSPGs play a vital regulator of heparin binding growth factor signaling, e.g., FGF2, VEGF, HGF, PDGF, and heparin binding EGF (HB-EGF), also known as receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling (Lai et al., 2003).
evidence: This regulatory role is cited from published literature.

claim: Complete loss or markedly attenuated expression of SULF1 appeared in cancer cell lines derived from breast, pancreas, kidney, and hepatocellular cancers.
source: Complete loss or markedly attenuated expression of SULF1 appeared in cancer cell lines derived from breast, pancreas, kidney, and hepatocellular cancers, suggesting that downregulation of SULF1 is relatively common among epithelial cancers (Lai et al., 2008).
evidence: This pattern of SULF1 expression in cancers is cited from published literature.

claim: EZH2 was highly expressed in CH2879 and JJ012 chondrosarcoma cell lines compared to normal chondrocytes.
source: In contrast to normal chondrocytes, EZH2 was highly expressed in CH2879 and JJ012 chondrosarcoma cell lines as well as increased histone 3 trimethylation at lysine 27 (H3K27me3; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: H3K27me3 is increased in CH2879 and JJ012 chondrosarcoma cell lines compared to normal chondrocytes.
source: In contrast to normal chondrocytes, EZH2 was highly expressed in CH2879 and JJ012 chondrosarcoma cell lines as well as increased histone 3 trimethylation at lysine 27 (H3K27me3; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The expression of EZH2 correlates with poor survival of sarcoma patients.
source: Consistently, the expression of EZH2 correlated well with poor survival of sarcoma patients, and the justification of clinical relevance for EZH2 in chondrosarcoma by using tissue microarray was also shown later in Figure 8.
evidence: This correlation is shown through Kaplan-Meier survival analysis in Figure 1B.

claim: Knockdown of EZH2 reduced the proliferative capacity of chondrosarcoma cell lines.
source: Knockdown of EZH2 reduced the proliferative, migrated, and colony-forming capacity of chondrosarcoma cell lines (Figure 1E and I) and supporting the notion that EZH2 may have a role in chondrosarcoma development.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTS assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Knockdown of EZH2 reduced the migration capacity of chondrosarcoma cell lines.
source: Knockdown of EZH2 reduced the proliferative, migrated, and colony-forming capacity of chondrosarcoma cell lines (Figure 1E and I) and supporting the notion that EZH2 may have a role in chondrosarcoma development.
evidence: This is demonstrated by transwell migration assay data shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: Knockdown of EZH2 reduced the colony-forming capacity of chondrosarcoma cell lines.
source: Knockdown of EZH2 reduced the proliferative, migrated, and colony-forming capacity of chondrosarcoma cell lines (Figure 1E and I) and supporting the notion that EZH2 may have a role in chondrosarcoma development.
evidence: This is demonstrated by soft agar assay data shown in Figures 1H and 1I.

claim: 40 genes were both targeted by EZH2 and significantly dysregulated in JJ012 chondrosarcoma cell line compared to normal chondrocytes.
source: We first searched the genes that were both targeted by EZH2 (n=704) and associated with significant dysregulated genes from cDNA microarray in comparison with normal chondrocyte to JJ012 chondrosarcoma cell line (n=6771). Between these two pooled genes, 40 were overlapped.
evidence: This is shown by the Venn diagram analysis in Figure 2A combining ChIP-seq and microarray data.

claim: EZH2 is enriched at the SULF1 promoter in chondrosarcoma cell lines.
source: q-ChIP experiments further validated enrichment of EZH2 bound at Sulf1 promoter in various chondrosarcoma cell lines (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative ChIP assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SULF1 mRNA is downregulated in JJ012 and CH2879 chondrosarcoma cell lines compared to normal chondrocytes.
source: Consistently, qRT-PCR analysis showed that SULF1 was downregulated in chondrosarcoma cell lines, JJ012 and CH2879 as compared with normal chondrocyte (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: SULF1 protein expression is reduced in JJ012 and CH2879 chondrosarcoma cell lines compared to normal chondrocytes.
source: Immunoblotting also demonstrated that SULF1 expression was reduced in JJ012 and CH2879 cell lines (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Knockdown of EZH2 induces SULF1 expression in JJ012 and CH2879 cell lines.
source: Knockdown of EZH2 induced SULF1 expression in both JJ012 and CH2879 cell lines (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: Lower SULF1 expression significantly correlates with poorer survival in sarcoma populations.
source: To further investigate the prognostic significance of EZH2/SULF1 axis in sarcoma, the Kaplan-Meier Plotter indicated that lower SULF1 expression significantly correlated with poorer survival in sarcoma populations (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Ectopic expression of SULF1 inhibits chondrosarcoma cell proliferation.
source: SULF1 ectopic-expression inhibited chondrosarcoma cell proliferation (Figure 3B), migration (Figure 3C), and colony-forming capacity (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Ectopic expression of SULF1 inhibits chondrosarcoma cell migration.
source: SULF1 ectopic-expression inhibited chondrosarcoma cell proliferation (Figure 3B), migration (Figure 3C), and colony-forming capacity (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transwell migration assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ectopic expression of SULF1 inhibits chondrosarcoma colony-forming capacity.
source: SULF1 ectopic-expression inhibited chondrosarcoma cell proliferation (Figure 3B), migration (Figure 3C), and colony-forming capacity (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Knockdown of SULF1 in SULF1-overexpressing cells restores colony-forming capacity.
source: Chondrosarcoma cells with ectopic-expressed SULF1 were re-introduced control and specific SULF1 shRNA and followed by the test of colony-forming assay. The colony-forming capacity was restored in the presence of SULF1 shRNA as compared with control (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Stable transfection of CH2879 cells with SULF1 markedly represses the growth of chondrosarcoma tumors in nude mice.
source: The stable transfection of CH2879 cells with SULF11 markedly repressed the growth of chondrosarcoma tumors with smaller size and weight compared with the control counterparts (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor xenograft data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Phosphorylation of cMET is decreased in SULF1 overexpressing chondrosarcoma cell lines.
source: To understand the mechanism of SULF1-mediated inhibitory effects on the tumorigenesis of chondrosarcoma cell lines, the unbiased RTK antibody array was performed and revealed that several phosphorylation of RTKs were decreased in SULF1 overexpression cell lines, with the largest fold decreases in cMET, and followed by ALK and TIE2 (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phospho-RTK antibody array data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Phosphorylation of ALK is decreased in SULF1 overexpressing chondrosarcoma cell lines.
source: To understand the mechanism of SULF1-mediated inhibitory effects on the tumorigenesis of chondrosarcoma cell lines, the unbiased RTK antibody array was performed and revealed that several phosphorylation of RTKs were decreased in SULF1 overexpression cell lines, with the largest fold decreases in cMET, and followed by ALK and TIE2 (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phospho-RTK antibody array data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Phosphorylation of TIE2 is decreased in SULF1 overexpressing chondrosarcoma cell lines.
source: To understand the mechanism of SULF1-mediated inhibitory effects on the tumorigenesis of chondrosarcoma cell lines, the unbiased RTK antibody array was performed and revealed that several phosphorylation of RTKs were decreased in SULF1 overexpression cell lines, with the largest fold decreases in cMET, and followed by ALK and TIE2 (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phospho-RTK antibody array data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Ectopic expression of SULF1 reduces phosphorylation of AKT, ERK1/2, and p38 in chondrosarcoma cell lines.
source: Western blotting analysis indicated that in cells with ectopic expression of SULF1, phosphorylation of cMET, AKT, ERK1/2, and p38 was reduced (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: EPZ-6438 treatment upregulates SULF1 expression in a dose-dependent manner in chondrosarcoma cell lines.
source: The expression of SULF1 in chondrosarcoma cell lines treated with EPZ-6438 (tazemetostat), an EZH2 inhibitor which reduced the enzymatical activity of EZH2 without affecting its expression, was explored by western blotting. The expression of SULF1 was upregulated in a dose-dependent manner with EPZ-6438 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: EPZ-6438 treatment reduces phosphorylation of cMET accompanied by upregulation of SULF1.
source: Additionally, phosphorylation of cMET was reduced accompanied with the augmentation of SULF1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Depletion of EZH2 decreases phosphorylation of cMET in chondrosarcoma cell lines.
source: We also tested whether the loss of EZH2, which induces SULF1 expression, would impair cMET phosphorylation in chondrosarcoma cell lines. The phosphorylation of cMET was vigorously decreased while depletion of EZH2 in chondrosarcoma cell line (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The enzymatic activity of SULF1 is required for dephosphorylation of cMET.
source: The CA mutant of SULF1 lost enzymatic activity and was unable to repress the phosphorylation of cMET compared to the ectopic expressed WT SULF1 in CH2879 (Figure 4F), suggesting that sulfatase enzymatic activity of SULF1 was required for the dephosphorylation of cMET.
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data comparing wild-type and CA mutant SULF1 shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Wild-type SULF1 reduces proliferation of chondrosarcoma cells while CA mutant SULF1 does not.
source: Overexpression of WT SULF1 reduced the proliferation (Figure 4G) and colony forming ability in vitro (Figure 4H), as expected from the reduced phosphorylation of cMET in Figure 4F. In contrast, CA mutant SULF1 which lost enzymatic activity failed to do so in chondrosarcoma cell line (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Wild-type SULF1 inhibits tumor development in vivo while CA mutant shows partial tumor suppression activity.
source: The results indicated that WT SULF1, associated with full sulfatase activity inhibited tumor development, consistent to what was observed in vitro culture. But the CA mutant, which lost sulfatase activity, thought to recover tumorigenicity, still associated with partial tumor suppression activity as it could not completely recover tumor volume similar to that of vector control (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor xenograft data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Higher cMET expression is associated with poorer survival of patients with sarcoma.
source: Additionally, higher cMET expression associated with poorer survival of patient with sarcoma was also observed (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The interaction between cMET and CD44 is abolished in SULF1 overexpressed chondrosarcoma cell lines.
source: The interaction between cMET and CD44 was clearly detected by immunoprecipitation analysis in vector control chondrosarcoma cell lines as reported, yet such interaction between cMET and CD44 was abolished in SULF1 overexpressed chondrosarcoma cell lines (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Ectopic expression of SULF1 diminishes cell surface staining for N-sulfated glucosamine containing HSGAGs.
source: The ectopic expressed SULF1 of chondrosarcoma cell lines showed the cell surface staining for N-sulfated glucosamine containing HSGAGs was diminished compared with vector control chondrosarcoma cell lines via using flow cytometry analysis (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: Sulfated HSGAGs are reduced in SULF1 ectopic expressed cell lines compared to vector control.
source: Furthermore, western blot of sulfated HSGAGs in SULF1 ectopic expressed cell line was reduced in contrast to the counterpart (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Tivantinib, crizotinib, and capmatinib effectively attenuate the phosphorylation of cMET in chondrosarcoma cell lines.
source: Tivantinib, crizotinib, and capmatinib effectively attenuated the phosphorylation of cMET in both CH2879 and JJ012 chondrosarcoma cell lines (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Tivantinib and crizotinib decrease the phosphorylation of cMET at low dosages (0.4 and 0.3 μM, respectively).
source: Particularly, tivantinib and crizotinib decreased the phosphorylation of cMET with low dosage at 0.4 and 0.3 μM, respectively (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Tivantinib and crizotinib reduce colony forming capacity in CH2879 and JJ012 cell lines.
source: Reduction of colony forming capacity was also observed in both CH2879 and JJ012 cell lines by treating with tivantinib and crizotinib (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by colony formation assay data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: Crizotinib treatment inhibits cartilage tumor growth in orthotopic immunodeficiency mice in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Crizotinib treatment inhibited cartilage tumor growth in orthotopic immunodeficiency mice in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 7B and C) without altering the mice body weight during administrated vehicle or crizotinib (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by bioluminescent imaging and tumor volume measurements shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: Crizotinib treatment does not alter mice body weight during administration.
source: Crizotinib treatment inhibited cartilage tumor growth in orthotopic immunodeficiency mice in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 7B and C) without altering the mice body weight during administrated vehicle or crizotinib (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by body weight measurements shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Crizotinib therapy decreases the phosphorylation of cMET in mice tumors.
source: Moreover, western blotting was shown that crizotinib therapy could decrease the phosphorylation of cMET in mice tumors (Figure 7F), which results in attenuating chondrosarcoma progression and dramatically ameliorate survival (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data from tumor samples shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Crizotinib treatment dramatically ameliorates survival in chondrosarcoma-bearing mice.
source: Moreover, western blotting was shown that crizotinib therapy could decrease the phosphorylation of cMET in mice tumors (Figure 7F), which results in attenuating chondrosarcoma progression and dramatically ameliorate survival (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival curve data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Chondrosarcoma patient samples exhibit low-level expression of SULF1 compared to normal tissue.
source: As a result, the patient samples exhibited a low-level expression of SULF1 and high-level expression of EZH2, and phospho-cMET compared to their counterpart (Figure 8A-C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Chondrosarcoma patient samples exhibit high-level expression of EZH2 compared to normal tissue.
source: As a result, the patient samples exhibited a low-level expression of SULF1 and high-level expression of EZH2, and phospho-cMET compared to their counterpart (Figure 8A-C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Chondrosarcoma patient samples exhibit high-level expression of phospho-cMET compared to normal tissue.
source: As a result, the patient samples exhibited a low-level expression of SULF1 and high-level expression of EZH2, and phospho-cMET compared to their counterpart (Figure 8A-C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: DZNep attenuates EZH2 protein expression and decreases H3K27me3, promoting cell death of chondrosarcoma cell lines by apoptosis.
source: The compound, DZNep, was shown to attenuate EZH2 protein expression and subsequently decreased H3K27me3, resulted in promoting cell death of chondrosarcoma cell line by apoptosis (Girard et al., 2014).
evidence: This mechanism of DZNep is cited from published literature.

claim: Downregulation of SULF1 in multiple cancers is orchestrated by DNA hypermethylation of CpG islands within the promoter or exon 1A.
source: Evidence has been demonstrated that downregulation of SULF1 in multiple cancers including ovarian, breast, gastric, and hepatoma is orchestrated by DNA hypermethylation of CpG islands which located within promoter or exon 1 A to prevent the transcription factors from binding to their DNA binding sites (Lai et al., 2004b; Lai et al., 2004a; Staub et al., 2007), concluding that epigenetic modulation was crucial for SULF1 silencing in cancer cells.
evidence: This epigenetic mechanism is cited from published literature.

claim: cMET facilitates migration of chondrosarcoma cell lines upon HGF interaction.
source: cMET has been reported to facilitate migration of chondrosarcoma cell lines upon HGF interaction (Tsou et al., 2013).
evidence: This functional role of cMET is cited from published literature.

claim: CD44 is highly expressed on the surface of chondrocytes and is a receptor for hyaluronan.
source: Prior investigation demonstrated that CD44 was highly expressed in surface of chondrocytes and was a receptor for hyaluronan.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CD44 expression and function.

claim: TNF-α induces sulfation of CD44 to change it from inactive to active form.
source: For instance, the proinflammatory cytokine like tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) was illustrated to change the inactive form of CD44 into active form via induction of the sulfation of CD44 (Maiti et al., 1998).
evidence: This regulatory mechanism is cited from published literature.

claim: Integrated multi-omics classification reveals the significance of the loss of expression of the 14q32 locus in defining malignancy of cartilage tumors.
source: For instance, Nicolle et al., 2019 indicated that integrated multi-omics classification to reveal the significance of the loss of expression of the 14q32 locus in defined malignancy on cartilage tumors.
evidence: This finding is cited from published literature.

claim: IDH activating mutations drive genome-wide hypermethylation in chondrosarcoma contributing to activation of proliferative and glycolytic state driven by HIF.
source: The IDH activating mutations driving a genome-wide hypermethylation in chondrosarcoma contribute to the activation of proliferative and glycolytic state, which was potentially driven by the hypoxia inducible factor (Nicolle et al., 2019).
evidence: This molecular mechanism is cited from published literature.

claim: HIF-2α is a critical regulator for tumor growth, local invasion, and metastasis in chondrosarcoma.
source: The other group uncovered that HIF-2α as a critical regulator for tumor growth, local invasion, and metastasis in chondrosarcoma by using weighted gene co-expression network analysis (Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: This regulatory role is cited from published literature.

claim: Combination of HIF-2α inhibitor with chemotherapy agents synergistically promotes chondrosarcoma cell apoptosis and abrogates malignant features in mice.
source: They also demonstrated that combination with small molecule HIF-2α inhibitor and chemotherapy agents synergistically promoted chondrosarcoma cell apoptosis and abrogates the malignant features of chondrosarcoma in mice.
evidence: This therapeutic combination effect is cited from published literature.

claim: 3D cell culture models show more resistance to chemotherapeutic drugs and targeted therapeutic agents compared to 2D culture systems.
source: Recently, Palubeckaite and colleagues have generated an alginate-based 3D cell culture model of chondrosarcoma to evaluate the treatment of chemotherapeutic drugs and target therapeutic agents including Sapanisertib (mTOR inhibitor) and AGI-519 (inhibitor of mutant IDH1). They reported that more resistant results of those treatment were observed in 3D compared to 2D cell culture system (Palubeckaitė et al., 2020).
evidence: This comparison of 2D vs 3D culture systems is cited from published literature.

claim: Inhibition of mTOR alone in 3D culture system shows lower effectiveness and might be improved by combination treatment.
source: Inhibition of mTOR alone in this 3D system was showed lower effectiveness and which might be improved by combination treatment to eliminate the remining cell population (Boehme et al., 2018).
evidence: This therapeutic observation is cited from published literature.

claim: AGI-5198 shows reduction of clonogenic capacity only after long-term treatment under high concentrations in 3D culture models.
source: Previous investigations reported that using 3D culture model was reduction of clonogenic capacity only after long-term treatment under high concentrations, yet no benefit of treatment was detected at lower concentrations or shorter treatment times (Li et al., 2015; Suijker et al., 2015).
evidence: This treatment response pattern is cited from published literature.

claim: Ivosidenib (AGI-120) demonstrated poor progression-free survival with single agent therapy in retrospective investigation.
source: Improved version of IDH mutation inhibitor, ivosidenib (AGI-120), increased the metabolical stability and was approved for chondrosarcoma clinical trial (Popovici-Muller et al., 2018). However, it was demonstrated poor progression-free survival with only one agent therapy in the retrospective investigation (van Maldegem et al., 2019).
evidence: This clinical trial outcome is cited from published literature.

claim: Tivantinib is a potent non-ATP competitive selective and oral c-Met small molecule inhibitor currently under evaluation in clinical trials for liver and lung cancers.
source: Suggesting that the limiting effects on the target therapies in chondrosarcoma thus far, tivantinib (ARQ-197) is a potent non-ATP competitive selective and oral c-Met small molecule inhibitor currently under evaluation of clinical trial for liver and lung cancers (Michieli and Di Nicolantonio, 2013).
evidence: This drug characterization is cited from published literature.

claim: Crizotinib is a type Ia tyrosine kinase inhibitor approved for treatment of ALK or ROS1-rearranged advanced non-small cell lung cancers.
source: Crizotinib is a type Ia tyrosine kinase inhibitor that is approved for the treatment of ALK or ROS1-rearranged advanced non-small cell lung cancers (Goździk-Spychalska et al., 2014).
evidence: This drug approval status is cited from published literature.

claim: Crizotinib has potent activity against cMET in addition to ALK and ROS1.
source: In addition to its activity against ALK and ROS1, it has potent activity against cMET and low nanomolar potency in cell lines including our studies.
evidence: This drug activity profile is stated based on known pharmacology and supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: The EZH2/SULF1/cMET axis provides a therapeutic potential for development of effective target therapy to treat chondrosarcoma.
source: The results not only established a signal pathway promoting malignancy of chondrosarcoma but also provided a therapeutic potential for further development of effective target therapy to treat chondrosarcoma.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reduction of SULF1 cannot remove the 6-O sulfation in HSPG resulting in stabilization of HGF, cMET, and CD44 tricomplex.
source: In chondrosarcoma, the expression of EZH2 was upregulated and thereby inhibited the SULF1 expression. Reduction of SULF1 cannot remove the 6-O sulfation in HSPG resulting in the stabilization of HGF, cMET, and CD44 tricomplex to activate the downstream signaling such as phosphorylation of AKT, p38, and ERK (Figure 8D).
evidence: This mechanistic model is inferred from the experimental data and illustrated in Figure 8D.

claim: Stabilization of HGF, cMET, and CD44 tricomplex activates downstream signaling including phosphorylation of AKT, p38, and ERK.
source: In chondrosarcoma, the expression of EZH2 was upregulated and thereby inhibited the SULF1 expression. Reduction of SULF1 cannot remove the 6-O sulfation in HSPG resulting in the stabilization of HGF, cMET, and CD44 tricomplex to activate the downstream signaling such as phosphorylation of AKT, p38, and ERK (Figure 8D).
evidence: This signaling cascade is demonstrated by western blot data and illustrated in the model in Figure 8D.

claim: The IC50 of capmatinib (12 μM) is much higher than tivantinib (1 or 1.2 μM) and crizotinib (0.5 μM) in chondrosarcoma cell lines.
source: For cMET inhibitors, the IC50 of campatinib (12 μM) was much higher than tivantinib (1 or 1.2 μM) and crizotinib (0.5 μM) in chondrosarcoma cell lines (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IC50 determination data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: EZH2 inhibitors GSK343 and EPZ-6438 require higher IC50 concentrations to diminish H3K27me3 and colony-forming ability compared to cMET inhibitors.
source: In contrast to cMET inhibitors, EZH2 inhibitor required higher IC50 concentrations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) to diminish trimethylation of histone lysine 27 (H3K27me3; Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and colony-forming ability (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E) in chondrosarcoma cell lines.
evidence: This comparison is demonstrated by dose-response data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The SULF1 level in transfected chondrosarcoma cell lines is comparable to the expression level of SULF1 in primary normal chondrocytes.
source: It is worth to mention that the SULF1 level in the transfected chondrosarcoma cell lines are comparable to the expression level of SULF1 in primary normal chondrocytes (n=107) by using qRT-PCR analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This comparison is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The phosphorylation of Y1003 of cMET has been implicated to associate with tumor suppressive activity.
source: The phosphorylation of Y1003 of cMET has been implicated to associate tumor suppressive activity (Organ and Tsao, 2011).
evidence: This functional association is cited from published literature.

claim: CA mutant SULF1 shows gain of phosphorylation of Y1003 of cMET in tumors but not in in vitro cell culture.
source: However, unexpectedly, the gain of phosphorylation of Y1003 of cMET was markedly detected in tumors, but not in the in vitro cell culture (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This differential phosphorylation pattern is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CA mutant SULF1 retains similar phosphorylation profile of Y1234/1235 of cMET in cell lysates and tumors.
source: We examined the different phosphorylation site of cMET and found that CA mutant retained the similar phosphorylated profile of Y1234/1235 of cMET, a catalytic activation site, in cell lysates and tumors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This phosphorylation pattern is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The EZH2/SULF1 axis regulation is also observed in osteosarcoma cell lines.
source: This regulation of EZH2/SULF1 axis was also observed in the other sarcoma cells such as osteosarcoma cell lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot and functional assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Similar expression patterns of EZH2, SULF1, and phospho-cMET observed in chondrosarcoma are also found in osteosarcoma tissue samples.
source: These similar results were also observed in osteosarcoma tissue samples (n=31; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.
